# What "learning" means {#sec-ch01}

Anyone who starts learning AI today hears many new words at once: machine learning, deep learning, LLM, RAG, agents. It feels like seven different subjects. But all these words belong to one story. Each new idea came because the old idea had a problem it could not solve.

In this chapter we go through that story from the beginning, in simple steps. At the end, you will see where this book fits.

::: {.goals}
- Understand the difference between a computer that follows rules and a computer that learns.
- Explain what a *model* is, in one sentence.
- See the full picture: AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs, RAG, agents and Jev.
:::

## Rules work, until they don't

Many systems in our daily life follow simple rules. A water tank switch turns the motor off when the tank is full. Your bank blocks a UPI payment if it is above your daily limit. A college portal shows "absent" if attendance is below 75%. Nobody "trained" these systems. A programmer wrote the rule, and the computer follows it.

Rules are good. They are fast and cheap, and when something goes wrong you can read the rule and understand why. If a simple rule solves your problem, use the rule.

The problem starts when the situation keeps changing. Think about fake messages that try to steal passwords. This is called **phishing**. The IT team of a company writes a rule: *if an email has the word "password", mark it as suspicious.* On Monday, the rule blocks the IT team's own "reset your password" emails, so they add an exception. On Wednesday, the attacker writes "passw0rd" with a zero, so they add another rule. On Friday, the attacker stops using the word completely and just sends a link to a fake login page. The list of rules keeps growing, and it is always one step behind the attacker. You may have seen the same thing with fake "KYC update" SMS messages: the wording changes every week.

![Two ways to catch phishing. On the left, every new trick forces a new exception, and the list never catches up. On the right, we stop writing rules and show the computer labelled examples instead.](/figures/ch01/rules-vs-examples.pdf){#fig-rules-vs-examples}

So we change the approach. Instead of writing the rules ourselves, we collect thousands of old emails where we already know the answer: this one was phishing, this one was normal. Then we ask the computer to find the pattern by itself (@fig-rules-vs-examples).

::: {.keyidea}
**A computer can learn the rules by itself from examples.** We do not write every rule by hand. We show it thousands of old cases where we already know the answer, and it finds the pattern. When the cheaters change their tricks, we simply show it new examples.
:::

## What is a model?

After the computer studies the examples, we get something we can use on new cases. You give it a new email, and it gives back an answer. This thing is called a **model**.

You can imagine a model as a machine with many small knobs. During learning, the computer keeps turning the knobs until the machine gives the right answer for most of the examples. After that, we stop turning the knobs and use the machine on new emails, where nobody knows the answer yet.

::: {.keyidea}
**A model is a learned rule.** It is like a formula whose numbers were not typed by a programmer but found from examples. You give it a new case, and it gives back an answer.
:::

You already use many models. When your bank sends an SMS like *"Did you just make a payment of ₹40,000 in another city? Reply NO if not you,"* no person wrote a rule about you. A model learned your normal spending pattern, and this payment did not match it.

## A model can learn the wrong thing

To make the ideas concrete, this book follows one example all the way through: Kestrel Logistics, the company from the prologue, whose computers raise **alerts** whenever something looks suspicious. Suppose that in four weeks the security team receives {{< num ch01 n_alerts int >}} alerts, about {{< num ch01 per_day int >}} per day, and only {{< num ch01 base_rate pct1 >}} of them are real attacks; the rest are false alarms. Since this is an example, we can assume we know the correct answer for every alert, which lets us check every idea properly.

Each alert comes with a *threat score* between 0 and 1. The score comes from outside security services that keep lists of known dangerous websites and computers. A high score means the alert involves something already known to be dangerous. Let us try a simple rule: *if the score is above some number t, mark the alert as an attack.* A cut-off number like *t* is called a **threshold**.

Which value of *t* should we choose? We let the computer try every value from 0 to 1, count the mistakes for each value, and keep the value with the fewest mistakes. This is learning in its simplest form, where we try many settings on the examples and keep the one that works best.

![Every possible threshold and the mistakes it makes. Low thresholds bury the team in false alarms; high ones miss attacks. The total is lowest at the far right, just below the dotted line for "flag nothing at all".](/figures/ch01/threshold-search.pdf){#fig-threshold-search}

The computer chooses {{< num ch01 best_t f2 >}}. With this threshold it makes {{< num ch01 best_mistakes int >}} mistakes. Yet a rule that *never* marks anything as an attack makes {{< num ch01 never_flag_mistakes int >}} mistakes, almost the same number. Out of {{< num ch01 attacks int >}} real attacks, the "best" rule catches only {{< num ch01 best_caught int >}} (@fig-threshold-search).

Why did this happen? There are about twelve harmless alerts for every real attack. So the easiest way to reduce the number of mistakes is to almost never raise an alarm. The computer did exactly what we asked. Our question was wrong.

::: {.keyidea}
**If you ask the wrong question, you get a useless answer.** We asked the computer only to "make as few mistakes as possible". Since attacks are rare, it learned the easiest trick, which is never to say "attack". The computer did what we asked, not what we wanted.
:::

In fact, our question had two problems. First, it counted every mistake as equal, although missing a real attack costs much more than one false alarm; Chapter 3 fixes this. Second, it forced the answer to be only *yes* or *no*, which throws away useful information, as we see next.

## A better answer: how likely?

Let us ask a different question: *among alerts with a similar score, how many were real attacks?*

![Group the alerts by threat score and count how many were real attacks. The share climbs steadily from 2% to 62%. Even at the top, plenty are harmless; even at the bottom, a few are attacks.](/figures/ch01/not-yes-no.pdf){#fig-not-yes-no}

@fig-not-yes-no shows the answer. There is no clear line where alerts suddenly become dangerous. Even in the lowest-score group, {{< num ch01 bottom_bin_rate pct >}} were attacks. That looks small, but the group has {{< num ch01 bottom_bin_n int >}} alerts, so more than a hundred attacks are hiding there. And in the highest-score group, only {{< num ch01 top_bin_rate pct >}} were attacks.

So for an alert with a score of 0.55, "attack" or "safe" is the wrong answer. A more useful answer would be *about one in five alerts like this is an attack.*

This kind of answer is much more useful. It tells the team how worried to be, which alerts to check first, and, once we know the cost of each mistake, where to draw the line.

::: {.keyidea}
**"How likely" is more useful than "yes" or "no".** An answer like "one in five alerts like this is an attack" tells you how worried to be and which case to check first. But it helps only if that "one in five" is true.
:::

When a model's "how sure" is correct, we say the model is **calibrated**. You will see this word many times in this book, and Chapter 2 explains it fully.

## The bigger story, and where this book fits

The threat score was one simple number. Real data is often much messier, and each new step in AI came to handle that:

- **Deep learning.** A photo has lakhs of pixels, and an email is a long piece of text. Nobody can write rules for these by hand. So researchers built models with many layers, which find their own clues in the raw data.
- **Large language models (LLMs).** Researchers then trained very large deep-learning models on a huge amount of text, with one simple task: guess the next word. To do this well, the models had to learn the language itself. ChatGPT is an LLM.
- **RAG.** An LLM knows a lot about the world, but nothing about your company. So before it answers, we search your company's documents and give it the right pages to read.
- **Agents.** Finally, we let the model use tools, such as searching, sending an email or closing a ticket, and work step by step towards a goal.

Chapters 4 and 5 explain each of these in more detail.

When you watch an agent work, you notice something interesting. Most of its steps are not writing. They are small decisions with only a few possible answers: *Is this alert real? Which team should handle this ticket? Is this action safe?* Today, people usually send each such question to an LLM. The LLM writes a full paragraph, and then another program has to search that paragraph for the actual answer. It works, but it is like asking someone to write an essay when you only wanted a tick in a box: slow and costly for such a small job.

![The same question, two ways. An LLM writes its answer piece by piece, and your code has to read the sentence. A decision model returns the answer as data, with a probability for every option, in one pass.](/figures/ch01/generate-vs-decide.pdf){#fig-generate-vs-decide}

In 2026, a company called TypeSafe AI released a model named **Jev** for these small decisions. Jev does not write any text. You give it the situation and a clear question, and it gives back the answer with a probability for each option (@fig-generate-vs-decide). TypeSafe calls it a *System One* model. The name comes from the psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who called our fast, automatic thinking "System 1" [@kahneman2011]. In this book, the numbers shown for Jev are examples to explain the ideas, not measurements of the real product. They are marked *synthetic*.

![The story so far. Each step exists because the one before it hit a problem it couldn't solve. System One models like Jev grow out of deep learning and fit into the "decide" step of an agent.](/figures/ch01/ai-story-map.pdf){#fig-ai-story-map}

@fig-ai-story-map shows the whole story on one page. The next two chapters stay with the basics, because everything else in the book depends on one idea: a good answer should say how likely it is, and that "how likely" should be correct.

1. Name one system you use that follows fixed rules, and one that has learned from examples. How did you know?
:::
